questions.question: From the labelled rabbit sperm diagram (options AW, BX, CY, DZ), state which structure contains the genetic information used to make acrosomal enzymes.
questions.answer: C: Y (the nucleus)
steps: Acrosomal enzymes are proteins, so the genetic information for them is the gene for each enzyme, which is DNA.
In a sperm cell the DNA is in the nucleus, the large rounded head region labelled Y.
W is the acrosome, which stores the enzymes but does not contain their genes, and Z is the midpiece with mitochondria, so neither is correct.

questions.question: Name the solid ball of genetically identical cells formed when a fertilised rabbit egg divides by mitosis.
questions.answer: Morula.
steps: Mitosis of the fertilised egg (zygote) gives many cells that remain packed together.
The cells are genetically identical because the DNA is copied exactly before each division.
The morula is a solid ball with no fluid-filled cavity.
This solid ball of cells is called a morula, which forms before the hollow blastocyst.

questions.question: Describe one form of epigenetic modification that could alter the activation of certain genes in rabbit cells.
questions.answer: DNA methylation: methyl groups are added to cytosine bases, which switches the gene off (or histone modification such as acetylation, which switches it on).
steps: Epigenetic modification changes gene expression without changing the base sequence of DNA.
DNA methylation adds methyl groups to cytosine bases, usually blocking transcription and switching the gene off.
Histone modification such as acetylation loosens chromatin, so transcription factors can reach the gene and switch it on.
Either change alters which genes are transcribed in a given cell type.

questions.question: Explain how cells in the rabbit embryo become specialised after epigenetic modification.
questions.answer: Epigenetic changes switch different genes on or off in each cell, so each cell type makes only the proteins it needs for its job.
steps: Cells in the embryo have the same DNA but receive different signals as they develop.
Epigenetic modifications silence some genes (for example by methylation) and activate others.
Each cell then transcribes and translates only its active genes, producing specialised proteins.
The epigenetic pattern is copied to daughter cells during mitosis, so the specialisation is maintained.

questions.question: Discuss how genes and the environment interact to produce the fur colour of three types of rabbit, using the table and the information that one enzyme is inactive at core body temperature.
questions.answer: Fur colour depends on the alleles for an enzyme that makes pigment, and for Himalayan rabbits also on temperature: the enzyme works only in cooler body parts.
steps: A gene codes for an enzyme that controls production of pigment in the fur; the allele combination (genotype) decides which version of the enzyme is made.
Black rabbits (CC, Cc^ch or Cc^a) have at least one C allele coding for a fully working enzyme, so pigment is made all over; C is dominant.
Albino rabbits (c^a c^a) have no working enzyme, so no pigment is made anywhere and the fur is white; the environment has no effect.
Himalayan rabbits (c^h c^h or c^h c^a) make an enzyme whose shape changes (it is denatured) at the warm core body temperature, so it is inactive over most of the body and the fur is white.
In the cooler extremities (ears, nose, paws, tail) the enzyme is active, so pigment is made and these parts are black.
So the phenotype of a Himalayan rabbit comes from the interaction of its genotype with temperature; c^h is dominant to c^a because c^h c^a rabbits are Himalayan.

questions.question: From four options (A 1.6 x 10^-2 m, B 1.6 x 10^2 m, C 1.6 x 10^-3 m, D 1.6 x 10^3 m), state the diameter of the blue poison dart frog egg cell.
steps: The table gives the diameter of the blue poison dart frog egg as 1600 um.
In standard form 1600 = 1.6 x 10^3, so the answer is option D.

questions.question: Calculate how many times larger the volume of the blue poison dart frog egg is than a human egg of volume 1.8 x 10^6 m^3, to two significant figures.
questions.answer: About 1.2 x 10^3 times larger (1200)
steps: Frog egg diameter = 1600 um, so radius = 800 um.
To two significant figures, the frog egg is 1.2 x 10^3 (1200) times larger.

questions.question: Explain the differences between the genetic material of a female human egg cell and a skin cell, which both contain a nucleus and the skin cell has 46 chromosomes.
questions.answer: The egg is haploid (23 chromosomes, one of each pair, from meiosis) while the skin cell is diploid (46 chromosomes, two copies of each gene, from mitosis).
steps: The egg cell is a gamete made by meiosis, so it has 23 chromosomes (haploid), one from each homologous pair.
The skin cell is a body cell made by mitosis, so it has 46 chromosomes (diploid) in homologous pairs.
The skin cell therefore has two alleles of each gene, while the egg has only one.
Crossing over and independent assortment in meiosis make each egg's allele combination different from the skin cell and from other eggs.

questions.question: Explain why the cells in the morula are genetically identical.
questions.answer: All morula cells come from repeated mitosis of one zygote; DNA is copied exactly before each division and shared equally.
steps: The morula forms by repeated mitosis of a single fertilised egg (zygote).
Before each division the DNA is replicated exactly, producing identical sister chromatids.
Mitosis separates the sister chromatids equally into two daughter nuclei, so each new cell has the same genotype.
Every cell in the morula therefore has the same genome as the original zygote.

questions.question: Name structure A, shown in the diagram of the three structures formed after fertilisation, which can be used as a source of pluripotent stem cells.
questions.answer: Blastocyst
steps: Structure A is a hollow ball of cells with an inner cell mass and an outer layer of trophoblast cells; this is a blastocyst.
It forms from the morula after more cell division and specialisation.
The inner cell mass contains the pluripotent embryonic stem cells.

questions.question: Suggest why injecting pluripotent stem cells may benefit a person who has had a severe heart attack, which kills heart muscle cells.
questions.answer: Pluripotent stem cells can differentiate into new heart muscle cells, replacing the cells killed in the heart attack.
steps: Pluripotent stem cells can differentiate into many cell types, including heart muscle cells (cardiomyocytes).
Injected cells can divide by mitosis to increase their numbers in the damaged area.
They differentiate into new heart muscle cells that replace those that died.
The new muscle cells can contract, which may restore some heart function.

questions.question: From the lettered options showing the correct order of mitosis for the plant cell diagrams, select the correct sequence.
questions.answer: C: C, D, B, E, A
steps: C shows a rounded nucleus with chromatin just beginning to condense (early prophase); D shows condensed chromosomes with no nuclear envelope (late prophase).
B shows the chromosomes spread across the middle of the cell (metaphase); E shows chromatids pulled to opposite poles (anaphase).
A shows two cells, each with chromosomes at the pole and a new cell wall (telophase and cytokinesis).
The order C, D, B, E, A matches row C.

questions.question: Explain the changes in DNA content of a cell during one cell cycle, as shown by the graph.
questions.answer: DNA content stays at 2 a.u., doubles to 4 a.u. in S phase, stays at 4 a.u., then halves to 2 a.u. when the cell divides.
steps: From 0 to about 6 hours the DNA content is constant at 2 a.u. (G1 of interphase, before replication).
From about 6 to 10 hours it rises steadily from 2 to 4 a.u., because DNA is replicated in S phase (semi-conservative replication).
From 10 to 15 hours it stays at 4 a.u. (G2, then prophase to anaphase), as each chromosome now has two sister chromatids and the cell has not yet divided.

At about 15 hours it falls sharply to 2 a.u., because the sister chromatids are separated into two daughter nuclei and the cell divides (end of mitosis and cytokinesis), so each daughter has 2 a.u. and the content then stays at 2.

questions.question: Complete the DNA content graph to show how it would change if the cell had undergone meiosis to form gametes.
questions.answer: Line rises from 2 to 4 a.u. (about 6 to 10 hours), stays at 4, falls to 2 a.u. after meiosis I, then falls to 1 a.u. after meiosis II and stays at 1.
steps: Continue the given line at 2 a.u., then draw the same rise from 2 to 4 a.u. over S phase (about 6 to 10 hours), because DNA is replicated before meiosis.
Keep the line at 4 a.u. during prophase I and metaphase I, then draw a sharp vertical drop to 2 a.u. at the end of meiosis I, when homologous chromosomes separate into two cells.
Keep the line at 2 a.u. briefly, then draw a second sharp vertical drop to 1 a.u. at the end of meiosis II, when sister chromatids separate into four cells.
Finish with a horizontal line at 1 a.u., half the original value, because each gamete is haploid.

questions.question: The harvest mouse has a body of 55 to 75 mm and a tail of 50 to 75 mm; the Indian flat-haired mouse has a body of 10 to 12 cm and a tail of 7 to 8 cm. Calculate the percentage difference in minimum total length of the Indian flat-haired mouse compared with the harvest mouse, to two significant figures.
steps: Minimum total length = minimum body length + minimum tail length.
Harvest mouse: 55 mm + 50 mm = 105 mm = 10.5 cm.
Flat-haired mouse: 10 cm + 7 cm = 17 cm.
Percentage difference compared with harvest mouse = (17 - 10.5) / 10.5 x 100 = 61.9%, which is 62% to two significant figures.

questions.question: Lipid droplets in mouse egg cells have a mean radius of 88 um. Which option gives the mean volume of a lipid droplet in mm^3? Options: A 2.85 x 10^-6, B 2.85 x 10^-3, C 2.85 x 10^3, D 2.85 x 10^6.
steps: Convert the radius to mm: 88 um = 88 x 10^-3 mm = 0.088 mm.
Option A (2.85 x 10^-6) is the same volume in cm^3, not mm^3.

questions.question: On the timeline diagram of structures formed after fertilisation in a mouse, draw a circle around the mouse morula and label it.
questions.answer: Circle the third picture in the mouse row (at Day 2, the ball of cells) and label it morula.
steps: The mouse row shows, from left, a zygote, a two-cell embryo, a solid ball of cells and a hollow ball with an inner cell mass.
The morula is the solid ball of many cells with no cavity, the third picture, at Day 2.
The fourth picture (Day 3) has a fluid-filled cavity and an inner cell mass, so it is a blastocyst, not a morula.

questions.topic: Events from Sperm Entry to Zygote
questions.question: Describe the events that occur after a sperm cell enters an egg cell, until a zygote is formed.
questions.answer: Cortical granules block other sperm; the egg completes meiosis II; the sperm and egg nuclei fuse to form a diploid zygote.
steps: The sperm nucleus enters the egg cytoplasm after the sperm and egg membranes fuse.
Cortical granules release enzymes that change the zona pellucida, blocking other sperm (cortical reaction).
The egg completes meiosis II, forming a haploid egg nucleus.
The male and female nuclei fuse, forming a diploid zygote nucleus.

questions.question: Lipid droplets were found within 10 nm of mitochondria in mouse egg cells. Suggest why.
questions.answer: Fatty acids released from the lipid droplets are quickly transferred to nearby mitochondria, which respire them to make ATP.
steps: Lipid droplets store triglycerides as an energy reserve for the developing egg.
Lipase breaks the triglycerides down into fatty acids and glycerol near the droplet.
Fatty acids are oxidised in the mitochondria (beta-oxidation) to acetyl CoA, which enters the Krebs cycle.
Being very close shortens the diffusion distance, so fatty acids reach the mitochondria quickly and ATP supply is maintained.

questions.question: Describe the events from a pollen grain landing on the stigma to the production of a triploid endosperm nucleus and a zygote, using the ovule diagram.
questions.answer: A pollen tube grows to the ovule; one male nucleus fuses with the egg to form the zygote, and the other fuses with two polar nuclei to form the triploid endosperm.
steps: The pollen grain lands on the stigma, absorbs water and germinates, growing a pollen tube down the style.
The tube nucleus guides growth of the tube through the micropyle of the ovule.
The generative nucleus divides by mitosis to form two male nuclei in the pollen tube.
The tube releases the two male nuclei into the embryo sac.
One male nucleus fuses with the egg nucleus, forming a diploid zygote (2n).
The other male nucleus fuses with the two polar nuclei, forming a triploid endosperm nucleus (3n).

questions.question: Explain how a flowering plant with several ovules produces seeds that are genetically different from each other.
questions.answer: Each ovule's egg and each pollen grain are made by meiosis with different allele combinations, so each fertilisation gives a seed with a unique genotype.
steps: Each ovule contains an egg cell produced by meiosis, which carries a unique combination of alleles.
Crossing over and independent assortment during meiosis create different allele combinations in each gamete.
Each pollen grain is also made by meiosis, so the male nuclei fertilising different ovules differ genetically.
Random fusion of different egg and pollen nuclei gives each seed a different combination of alleles.

questions.question: Which statement about rough endoplasmic reticulum is correct? Options: A has 70S ribosomes, B has 80S ribosomes, C forms vesicles surrounding phospholipids only, D forms vesicles surrounding polysaccharides only.
questions.answer: B (it has 80S large ribosomes).
steps: Rough ER has ribosomes attached to its surface, and eukaryotic ribosomes are 80S.
70S ribosomes are found in prokaryotes and in mitochondria and chloroplasts, so A is wrong.
Only the rough ER has ribosomes attached, so the statement must refer to it.
Rough ER vesicles carry proteins, not only phospholipids (C) or only polysaccharides (D), so both are wrong.

questions.question: Name a substance synthesised by the organelle labelled A in the student's diagram of part of a eukaryotic cell.
questions.answer: Glycoprotein (the Golgi apparatus also makes lysosomes, secretory vesicles and, in plants, cell wall polysaccharides)
steps: Organelle A is a stack of flattened membrane sacs next to the rough ER, which is the Golgi apparatus.
The Golgi modifies proteins that arrive from the rough ER, for example by adding carbohydrate to make glycoproteins.
Other acceptable substances are lysosomal enzymes (to form lysosomes), polysaccharides such as cell wall material in plants, and secretory enzymes.

questions.question: Name two structures that could be present inside the nucleus in the diagram.
questions.answer: Chromatin (DNA wound around histones) and the nucleolus.
steps: Chromatin is DNA wound around histone proteins, condensing into chromosomes during division.
The nucleolus is a dense region where ribosomal RNA is made and ribosome subunits are assembled.
The nucleolus is not surrounded by its own membrane.
Both lie inside the nuclear envelope, which encloses the nucleus.

questions.question: Explain how plant cells increase in size after cell division.
questions.answer: Water enters by osmosis and expands the permanent vacuole, raising turgor pressure and stretching the cell wall so the cell enlarges.
steps: The vacuole sap contains solutes that lower water potential, so water enters the cell by osmosis.
The water fills and expands the large permanent vacuole, increasing its volume.
Increased turgor pressure stretches the cell wall, which is flexible while it is extending.
New cytoplasm and cell wall material are made, so the cell increases in size.

questions.question: Suggest how the sticky proteins holding the desert ant sperm bundle together would have been secreted.
questions.answer: Made on ribosomes of the rough ER, modified and packaged by the Golgi, then released by exocytosis in secretory vesicles.
steps: Ribosomes on the rough ER synthesise the sticky protein polypeptide.
Transport vesicles carry the protein from the rough ER to the Golgi apparatus.
The Golgi modifies the protein and packages it into secretory vesicles.
The vesicles fuse with the cell surface membrane and release the protein by exocytosis.

questions.question: Comment on the results of an investigation comparing the speed of individual sperm with bundles of sperm in liquids of different resistance.
questions.answer: Sperm bundles swim faster than individual sperm at every resistance except 0.5 a.u.; bundle speed stays about 19 to 21 um s^-1, but individual sperm slow down as resistance rises.
steps: Individual sperm: speed rises from about 14 um s^-1 at 0 a.u. to about 20 at 0.5, then falls to about 14.5 at 1.5 and about 9.5 um s^-1 at 4.0 a.u.
Sperm bundles: speed stays high and fairly constant (about 18.5 to 21.5 um s^-1) whatever the resistance.
Bundles are faster at 0, 1.5 and 4.0 a.u. (the error bars do not overlap), but at 0.5 a.u. the error bars overlap, so there is probably no real difference.
The advantage of bundling grows as resistance rises: at 4.0 a.u. bundles are about 11 um s^-1 faster, more than twice the speed of single sperm.
This suggests that moving together lets the sperm cope with a thicker liquid, such as the female tract, so a bundle is more likely to reach the egg.

questions.question: Plot the result that, at the highest sperm concentration with damaged zona pellucida, the percentage polyspermy was 52%.
questions.answer: Draw a bar for damaged zona pellucida at the highest concentration (200 x 10^3 cm^-3), shaded dark grey like the key, with its top at 52% on the y-axis, next to the 100 bar.
steps: Use the key: the highest sperm concentration (200 x 10^3 cm^-3) is shaded dark grey.
In the damaged zona pellucida group draw a third bar to the right of the 100 bar, the same width as the others.
Make the top of the bar level with 52% (between 50 and 60 on the axis) and shade it dark grey.

questions.question: Explain the results of the investigation into damaged zona pellucida and sperm concentration on percentage polyspermy in mouse egg cells.
questions.answer: A damaged zona pellucida lets more than one sperm enter, so polyspermy is higher, and it rises with sperm concentration.
steps: With an intact zona pellucida polyspermy is low (about 2 to 3% at the lowest concentration, 17 to 18% at the two higher ones) because the zona pellucida (and cortical reaction) blocks extra sperm.

With a damaged zona pellucida polyspermy is much higher at the higher concentrations (about 33% at 100 and 52% at 200 x 10^3 cm^-3, against 17 and 18% for intact), because the zona no longer stops extra sperm entering.
Higher sperm concentration means more sperm reach each egg, so polyspermy increases with concentration; with a damaged zona pellucida it keeps rising, but with an intact one it levels off.
At the lowest concentration there is no difference between intact and damaged (about 2.5%), because so few sperm are present that two rarely reach the same egg.

questions.question: From the sperm cell diagram (options AW, BX, CY, DZ), state the part of the sperm where the organelle shown in the electron micrograph is found.
questions.answer: C: Y (the midpiece)
steps: The electron micrograph shows an organelle with folded inner membranes (cristae): a mitochondrion.
In a sperm cell the mitochondria are packed in the midpiece, behind the head, where they supply ATP for the tail.
Y points to the midpiece, so the answer is C.

questions.question: Describe the role of one organelle involved in the production of the digestive enzyme acrosin.
questions.answer: Golgi apparatus: modifies and packages the acrosin into vesicles that form the acrosome.
steps: Ribosomes on the rough ER synthesise the acrosin polypeptide.
Transport vesicles carry the polypeptide from the rough ER to the Golgi apparatus.
The Golgi modifies the enzyme and packages it into vesicles.
These vesicles form the acrosome, which stores acrosin for release at fertilisation.

questions.question: The investigation used 2500 egg cells per sample. Calculate the number of egg cells fertilised by sperm with 2.5 a.u. acrosin activity.
questions.answer: 800 egg cells
steps: From the graph, about 32% of egg cells were fertilised at 2.5 a.u. acrosin activity.
Number fertilised = 32 / 100 x 2500 = 800.

questions.question: Explain why a higher activity of the digestive enzyme acrosin resulted in a higher percentage of egg cells being fertilised.
questions.answer: Acrosin digests the zona pellucida around the egg, opening a path so more sperm reach and fuse with the egg membrane.
steps: Acrosin is released from the acrosome at the sperm head when it reaches the egg.
It digests the zona pellucida and outer layers surrounding the egg.
Higher activity makes a clearer path for sperm to reach the egg cell surface membrane.
More sperm can fuse with the egg, so a higher percentage of eggs are fertilised.

questions.question: State how to calculate the actual size of a fertilised egg cell drawing, given its magnification.
questions.answer: Actual size = image size / magnification.
steps: Measure the diameter of the drawing (the image size), using a ruler or the scale bar.
Use the magnification stated for the drawing.
Divide the image size by the magnification to get the actual size.
Keep units consistent, converting mm to um if needed.

questions.question: Suggest why a fertilised egg cell with damaged zona pellucida has three nuclei.
questions.answer: The damaged zona pellucida let two sperm enter (polyspermy), so two sperm nuclei plus the egg nucleus were present.
steps: The zona pellucida helps block entry of more than one sperm into the egg.
Damage to the zona pellucida weakens this block, so more than one sperm can reach the egg membrane.
The cortical reaction may also fail to stop further sperm entry.
Two sperm nuclei plus the egg nucleus give three nuclei, a sign of polyspermy.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term organ system.
questions.answer: A group of organs that work together to carry out a particular function.
steps: An organ is made of several tissues that together perform a specific function.
An organ system is a group of organs working together for a shared, larger function.
Organ systems work together to keep the whole body functioning.
For example, the female reproductive system includes the ovaries, oviducts and uterus, which together produce and carry gametes.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term tissue.
questions.answer: A group of similar cells that work together to carry out a specific function.
steps: A tissue is made of cells of the same or similar type.
These cells are grouped together so they can perform one function jointly.
Cells in a tissue are specialised for a shared job.
The ovary contains tissue that produces gametes.

questions.question: Complete the table to show the correct statement for each structure found in gametes, showing how gametes are specialised for their functions.
questions.answer: Flagellum: A; mitochondria: C; nucleus: D; zona pellucida: B
steps: The flagellum of a sperm moves, so it propels the male gamete towards the female gamete (A).
Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration, so they produce ATP (C).
The nucleus contains the DNA, which is linear in eukaryotic cells (D).
The zona pellucida is the layer around the egg that the cortical granule enzymes modify to stop more sperm entering (B).

questions.question: From the graph of DNA content in one cell during one cycle (options AJ, BK, CL, DM), state the part where DNA is replicated.
questions.answer: B: K
steps: DNA is replicated in S phase of interphase.
On the graph the DNA content rises steadily from 2 to 4 a.u. in section K, so K is where replication occurs.
J is before replication, L is the replicated DNA (G2 and early mitosis) and M is when the cell divides.

questions.question: From the graph (options AJ, BL, CM, DN), state the part where condensation of chromosomes would be completed.
questions.answer: B: L
steps: Chromosomes condense in prophase, and condensation is complete by metaphase, before the chromatids are separated.
On the graph the DNA content is 4 a.u. in section L, after replication and before the cell divides, so this covers G2, prophase and metaphase.
Section M is the sharp fall as chromatids separate and the cell divides, and J and N are interphase (2 a.u.).

questions.question: Name the stage of mitosis when spindle fibres begin to form.
questions.answer: Prophase.
steps: In prophase the centrioles move to opposite poles of the cell.
Spindle fibres (microtubules) begin to form between the poles, starting in prophase.
Spindle formation begins in prophase, before the nuclear envelope has fully broken down.
The nuclear envelope breaks down as the spindle forms.

questions.question: Explain the role of the spindle in mitosis.
questions.answer: Spindle fibres attach to centromeres and contract to pull sister chromatids to opposite poles, so each daughter cell gets identical chromosomes.
steps: Spindle fibres attach to the centromeres of the chromosomes at metaphase.
They contract, pulling the sister chromatids apart in anaphase.
The chromatids move to opposite poles of the cell.
Each daughter nucleus receives an identical set of chromosomes.

questions.question: Draw a plant cell undergoing cell division, showing it just after mitosis has finished.
questions.answer: Two nuclei at opposite ends of the cell, each with the same set of chromosomes, and a cell plate starting to form across the middle.
steps: Draw two separate nuclei, one at each end of the cell, after telophase.
Show the chromosomes decondensing, with each nucleus holding an identical set.
Draw a cell plate beginning to form across the centre of the cell, showing cytokinesis.
Label the nuclei and the cell plate.

questions.question: Describe how to determine the mitotic index of the root tip tissue shown in the photograph.
questions.answer: Count cells in mitosis and the total cells in several fields of view; mitotic index = (cells in mitosis / total cells) x 100.
steps: Count the cells in mitosis (prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase) in several fields of view.
Count the total number of cells in the same fields of view.
Divide the number in mitosis by the total number of cells.
Multiply by 100 to give a percentage, and average over the fields.

questions.question: The diploid form of a liverwort has 64 chromosomes and the haploid form has 32. Complete the diagram to show the chromosome number in the female and male gametes.
questions.answer: 32 chromosomes in each of the female and male gametes.
steps: Gametes are produced by meiosis, which halves the chromosome number.
The diploid form has 64 chromosomes, so the gametes have 64 / 2 = 32.
Mitosis preserves 64 in the diploid form; meiosis halves it.
Both female and male gametes are haploid with 32 chromosomes.

questions.question: Label the part of the liverwort life cycle diagram where meiosis would have occurred.
questions.answer: Write 'meiosis' on the arrow from the diploid form (64) to the spores (32).
steps: Meiosis halves the chromosome number from diploid to haploid.
In the life cycle the chromosome number falls from 64 (diploid form) to 32 in the spores.
So label the arrow between the diploid form and the spores as meiosis.

questions.question: From the diagram of nuclei in an ovule and a pollen tube (options AP, BQ, CS, DT), state which letter labels an ovule.
questions.answer: A: P
steps: An ovule is the structure that contains the embryo sac, egg cell and nuclei, inside the ovary; P labels this.
Q is an anther, S the polar nuclei and T the egg cell, so the answer is A.

questions.question: From the same diagram (options AP, BS, CT, DU), state which letter labels an egg cell (female gamete).
questions.answer: C: T
steps: The egg cell (female gamete) lies in the embryo sac at the micropyle end, with the synergids beside it.
T points to this cell at the bottom of the embryo sac, so the answer is C.

questions.question: From the same diagram (options AR, BS, CT, DU), state which letter labels a male nucleus.
questions.answer: D: U
steps: The male nuclei are carried in the pollen tube, which grows through the style to the micropyle.
U points to the dark nuclei inside the pollen tube at the micropyle, so the answer is D.
R is a pollen grain, not a nucleus in the tube.

questions.question: From the same diagram (options AR, BS, CT, DU), state which letter labels a polar nucleus.
questions.answer: B: S
steps: Polar nuclei are the two nuclei in the middle of the embryo sac.
S points to these two central nuclei, so the answer is B.
One male nucleus fuses with them to form the triploid endosperm nucleus.

questions.question: Describe the function of the tube nucleus in a pollen tube.
questions.answer: The tube nucleus controls the growth of the pollen tube and directs it towards the ovule.
steps: The tube nucleus sits at the growing tip of the pollen tube.
It controls the growth of the tube down the style.
It directs the tube through the micropyle towards the embryo sac.
It is not fused with the egg; the generative nuclei carry out fertilisation.

questions.question: From the cell diagram at the start of metaphase I (options A centriole, B lysosome, C nucleolus, D ribosome), state which is organelle T.
questions.answer: A: centriole
steps: Organelle T is at the pole of the cell where the spindle fibres meet.
Centrioles lie at the poles and organise the spindle fibres (microtubules).
A lysosome, nucleolus or ribosome does not form the spindle, so the answer is A.

questions.question: Explain why chromatid A can be genetically different from chromatid B at metaphase I of meiosis.
questions.answer: Crossing over between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes in prophase I exchanges alleles, so the chromatids carry different genes.
steps: Homologous chromosomes pair up in prophase I to form bivalents.
Crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids, swapping equal segments of DNA.
The chromatids then carry different combinations of alleles.
So chromatids A and B can differ genetically even though they are on homologous chromosomes.

questions.question: Complete the student's drawings to show the four haploid cells produced by meiosis from the cell at metaphase I.
questions.answer: Four cells, each with one chromosome made of a single chromatid (like the drawn one): two cells with the dark chromosome and two with the light one.
steps: The cell at metaphase I has one homologous pair, each chromosome having two chromatids, so each haploid cell ends with one chromosome.
Meiosis II separates the sister chromatids, so each final cell contains a single chromatid (a single-stranded chromosome with a centromere), as in the first circle.
Draw one single chromatid in each of the other three circles.
Shade two cells like the dark chromosome and two like the light one, since the two homologues go into different cells (small pieces of the other shade may show crossing over).

questions.question: Explain how meiosis causes genetic variation in gametes.
questions.answer: Crossing over in prophase I and independent assortment of homologous pairs in metaphase I produce gametes with different allele combinations.
steps: In prophase I homologous chromosomes pair, and crossing over swaps segments between non-sister chromatids.
In metaphase I homologous pairs line up at random, so maternal and paternal chromosomes assort independently.
This produces many different combinations of alleles in each gamete.
So gametes differ from each other and from the parent cell.

questions.question: Give two differences in the arrangement of DNA at the beginning of interphase and at the end of prophase I of meiosis.
questions.answer: At the start of interphase DNA is unreplicated, uncondensed chromatin; at the end of prophase I it is replicated, condensed chromosomes of two chromatids paired with homologues.
steps: At the start of interphase the DNA is a single, uncoiled chromatin strand per chromosome, not yet replicated.
At the end of prophase I each chromosome has replicated and consists of two chromatids joined at a centromere.
At the end of prophase I the chromosomes are condensed and paired with their homologous partners as bivalents.
At the start of interphase the chromosomes are uncondensed and unpaired.

questions.question: Cell A (mitosis) and cell B (meiosis) both have 12 pg of DNA at prophase. What is the DNA mass in each daughter cell at the end of mitosis and at the end of meiosis?
questions.answer: 6 pg in each daughter cell after mitosis; 3 pg in each gamete after meiosis.
steps: At prophase the DNA has already replicated, so 12 pg is the replicated amount.
Mitosis gives two daughter cells, each with half: 12 / 2 = 6 pg.
Meiosis halves DNA at meiosis I and again at meiosis II, so each gamete has 12 / 4 = 3 pg.
The mitotic daughters are diploid (6 pg) and the gametes are haploid (3 pg).

questions.question: Plants can produce seeds by cross-fertilisation or self-fertilisation. Some plants prevent self-fertilisation: date palms have only male or only female flowers, and some orchids release chemicals that stop pollen from the same plant germinating. Others still produce seeds if cross-fertilisation has not occurred: fireweed self-fertilises, and unfertilised egg cells of a dandelion develop into a seed. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of the strategies used by date palms, orchids, fireweed and dandelions to promote or ensure seed production.
questions.answer: Outcrossing strategies give variation but depend on pollinators; self-fertilisation and asexual seed production ensure seeds but reduce variation and adaptability.
steps: Date palm has separate male and female plants, forcing cross-fertilisation, which increases variation and reduces harmful recessive alleles.
Disadvantage: pollen must be carried between plants, so pollination can fail and seed output is uncertain.
Orchids release chemicals that stop pollen from the same plant germinating, which prevents inbreeding but wastes some pollen.
Fireweed self-fertilises when cross-fertilisation fails, guaranteeing seeds, but offspring have less variation and may be less able to adapt.
Dandelion produces seeds from unfertilised eggs (apomixis), so seeds form without pollination, but the offspring are clones with no variation.
Overall, outcrossing gives variation and adaptability but risks failed pollination, while self-fertilisation or apomixis secures seed production at the cost of variation.

questions.question: Complete the diagram of one pair of homologous chromosomes to show them after crossing over has occurred.
questions.answer: Swap the ends of the two inner (non-sister) chromatids, so that each of these chromatids is part shaded and part unshaded; the outer chromatids stay unchanged.
steps: Crossing over happens between non-sister chromatids of the homologous chromosomes, at the place shown by the arrows.
On the left chromosome shade the top of the inner chromatid white, and on the right chromosome shade the matching top of the inner chromatid grey (the ends are exchanged).
The other two chromatids (the outer ones) stay completely grey on the left and completely white on the right.
Each exchanged chromatid is then a mixture of grey and white, showing new combinations of alleles.

questions.question: From the photograph of cells undergoing mitosis (options AP, BQ, CR, DS), state which cell is in prophase.
questions.answer: B: Q
steps: Prophase shows condensed chromosomes as a tangle of threads, spread through the cell before they line up.
Q shows such a tangle in a rounded cell, so Q is in prophase.
P is metaphase (chromosomes in a band across the middle), R is anaphase (two sets of chromosomes separating) and S is telophase (two separate groups of chromosomes).

questions.question: In embryo cells interphase lasts an average of nine hours. Using the diagram of relative proportions of the cell cycle, calculate how long cytokinesis would take.
questions.answer: 0.5 hours (30 minutes)
steps: Interphase takes 270 degrees of the circle, which is 9 hours, so 1 degree = 9 / 270 = 0.033 hours.
Cytokinesis takes 15 degrees = 15 x 0.033 = 0.5 hours.

questions.question: Calculate the total number of cells resulting from one cell dividing by mitosis eight times.
steps: Each mitosis doubles the number of cells.
After eight divisions, the number is 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 2^8.
Each division doubles the number of cells, so the count grows exponentially.

questions.question: At which stage of mitosis do the spindle fibres contract? Options: A anaphase, B metaphase, C prophase, D telophase.
questions.answer: A (anaphase).
steps: In anaphase the centromeres divide and the spindle fibres shorten.
Shortening of the fibres pulls the sister chromatids to opposite poles.
Vincristine stops the spindle shortening, so anaphase is the stage it affects.
In metaphase the fibres are attached but not yet contracting, and in prophase they are only forming.

questions.question: Evaluate the effectiveness of resveratrol, SRT1720 and vincristine in killing cancer cells, using the graph of the investigation.
questions.answer: SRT1720 with vincristine is the most effective (about 84% killed); vincristine alone kills about 51%, but resveratrol with vincristine (about 32%) is worse than vincristine alone.
steps: Used alone, vincristine is much the most effective drug (about 51% of cancer cells killed), while resveratrol (about 17%) and SRT1720 (about 9%) kill few.
Adding SRT1720 to vincristine raises the kill from about 51% to about 84%; the error bars do not overlap, so the increase is probably real and this is the best treatment.
Adding resveratrol to vincristine lowers the kill from about 51% to about 32%, so it makes vincristine less effective.

The error bar for vincristine alone is large (about 46 to 57%), so that result is less precise; the data do not show effects on healthy cells or side effects, or cover other cancers, so more tests are needed.

questions.question: From the yeast micrographs (options AJ, BK, CL, DM), state which structure identifies yeast as a eukaryote.
questions.answer: A: J
steps: A eukaryotic cell has membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum or Golgi apparatus, which prokaryotes lack.
J points to a membrane-bound organelle in the cytoplasm, so it identifies yeast as eukaryotic.
K and M are the outer wall or membrane layers, which prokaryotes also have, and L is cytoplasm.

questions.question: Explain why structure J can be seen using the electron microscope but not the light microscope.
questions.answer: Structure J is smaller than the light microscope's resolution (about 200 nm), but the electron microscope's much shorter wavelength resolves it.
steps: The resolution of a light microscope is limited by the wavelength of visible light, about 200 nm.
Structure J is smaller than this limit, so the light microscope cannot separate it from nearby structures.
Electron microscopes use electrons with a much shorter wavelength, giving much higher resolution.
So structure J is resolved and can be seen with the electron microscope.

questions.question: Explain why the nuclear envelope cannot be seen as two membranes using this electron microscope.
questions.answer: The two membranes are closer together than this microscope's resolution, so they appear as a single membrane.
steps: The nuclear envelope consists of two membranes separated by a narrow gap of about 20 to 40 nm.
To see two separate membranes, the microscope must resolve a distance smaller than this gap.
The resolution of this microscope is not fine enough, so the two membranes blur into one.
A higher-resolution electron micrograph would be needed to show two membranes.

questions.question: Explain the importance of mitosis in budding of yeast cells.
questions.answer: Mitosis copies the parent's DNA exactly and gives the bud a full identical set of chromosomes, so the bud is a genetically identical clone.
steps: Before budding, the parent's DNA is replicated exactly during interphase.
Mitosis separates the chromosomes equally, so the bud receives a complete, identical copy of the genome.
The bud is therefore genetically identical to the parent, a clone produced by asexual reproduction.
Because no meiosis or fusion is needed, budding is quick and needs only one parent.

questions.question: Suggest why the availability of oxygen and nutrients determines the rate of budding in yeast.
questions.answer: Oxygen and nutrients supply aerobic respiration (ATP) and raw materials for DNA and protein synthesis, so limited supply slows the growth and division needed for budding.
steps: Aerobic respiration needs oxygen and glucose to release energy as ATP.
ATP powers DNA replication, protein synthesis and growth needed to make the bud.
Nutrients such as amino acids and nucleotides are raw materials for new cytoplasm, organelles and DNA.
If oxygen or nutrients are limited, the bud grows more slowly, so the rate of budding falls.

questions.question: Deduce the effect of age and sex on the number of cases of a cancer, from the graph of cases in a human population.
questions.answer: Cases rise with age in both sexes, and males have more cases than females in every age group from 40, the gap widening with age.
steps: Age: there are almost no cases below 40, then the number of cases per 100 000 rises with each older age group.
Males: increase continuously, from about 25 at 40 to 49 years to about 660 at 80+.
Females: increase to about 190 at 70 to 79 years, then fall slightly to about 155 at 80+.
Sex: males have more cases than females in every age group from 40 onwards, for example about 370 v 140 at 60 to 69 and about 660 v 155 at 80+, so the difference grows with age.

questions.question: A city has 2 million people, 3% of whom are males over 80. Calculate how many of these males would have this cancer, using the graph.
questions.answer: About 400 males (396)
steps: Number of males over 80 = 3% of 2 000 000 = 60 000.
From the graph, males aged 80+ have about 660 cases per 100 000 people.

questions.question: State why the cells in a tissue sample were stained before being viewed under a microscope to calculate the mitotic index.
questions.answer: The stain binds to the chromosomes/DNA, making them visible so cells in each stage of mitosis can be identified and counted.
steps: Unstained cells are almost transparent under a light microscope and hard to see.
A stain such as acetic orcein binds to DNA in the chromosomes, making them dark.
Stained chromosomes let the cells in each stage of mitosis be identified.
This allows the proportion of cells in mitosis (mitotic index) to be counted.

questions.question: Describe how the mitotic index of the tissue sample would be determined.
questions.answer: Count the cells in mitosis and the total cells in several fields of view; mitotic index = (cells in mitosis / total cells) x 100.
steps: Count the cells in mitosis in several fields of view under the microscope.
Count the total number of cells in the same fields of view.
Divide the number in mitosis by the total number of cells.
Multiply by 100 to give the mitotic index as a percentage.

questions.question: In which stage of mitosis do chromosomes start to condense? Options: A anaphase, B metaphase, C prophase, D telophase.
questions.answer: C (prophase).
steps: Chromosomes start to condense in prophase, as the chromatin coils tightly.
The condensed chromosomes become visible as shorter, thicker structures.
Prophase is the first stage of mitosis, when condensation starts.
Metaphase, anaphase and telophase come later in mitosis.

questions.question: Explain how preventing the condensation of chromosomes would affect the survival of a patient with this cancer, using the graph of mitotic index against percentage survival.
questions.answer: Preventing chromosome condensation would stop mitosis, lowering the mitotic index and so increasing survival (for example about 65% v 42% at 250 weeks).
steps: Chromosomes must condense in prophase so that they can be separated by the spindle; if they cannot condense, mitosis cannot be completed and the cancer cells cannot divide.
The tumour would grow more slowly and fewer cells would be in mitosis, so the mitotic index would fall.
The graph shows that patients with a low mitotic index have higher survival than those with a high one (about 65% v 42% at 250 weeks, and about 88% v 62% at 100 weeks).
So the treatment should increase the percentage survival of patients.

questions.question: Which processes occur during interphase? 1 cell growth; 2 genetic material is replicated; 3 organelles are synthesised. Options: A 1 only, B 1 and 2 only, C 2 and 3 only, D 1, 2 and 3.
steps: During interphase the cell grows in size.
The DNA is replicated in the S phase of interphase, ready for mitosis.
Organelles such as mitochondria and ribosomes are synthesised, so the cell has enough to divide.
All three processes occur in interphase, so the answer is D.

questions.question: Which row shows the correct sequence of the photographed stages in the cell cycle?
questions.answer: C: V, Z, X, Y, W
steps: V is interphase: a round nucleus with a nucleolus and no visible chromosomes.
Z is prophase (chromosomes condensing, nuclear envelope breaking down), X is metaphase (chromosomes in the middle of the cell) and Y is anaphase (chromatids pulled to opposite poles).
W is telophase, with two nuclei forming at the poles.
The sequence V, Z, X, Y, W is row C.

questions.question: Calculate the magnification of photograph W using the scale bar.
questions.answer: About x 750 (accept about 700 to 800)
steps: The scale bar represents 24 um; measured on the paper (printed at A4 size) it is about 18 mm long.
Convert to micrometres: 18 mm = 18 000 um.
Magnification = image length / actual length = 18 000 / 24 = 750, so about x 750.

questions.question: A tissue had 450 cells in mitosis and a mitotic index of 37.5%. Calculate the number of cells in interphase.
steps: Mitotic index = (cells in mitosis / total cells) x 100.
Cells in interphase = total cells - cells in mitosis = 1200 - 450 = 750.
This assumes all non-dividing cells are in interphase.

questions.question: Describe the events that occur during prophase of mitosis.
questions.answer: Chromosomes condense and become visible as pairs of chromatids; the nuclear envelope breaks down and spindle fibres form from centrioles moving to the poles.
steps: Chromatin coils and shortens, so the chromosomes condense and become visible.
Each chromosome is seen as two sister chromatids joined at the centromere.
The nuclear envelope and nucleolus break down.
Centrioles move to opposite poles and spindle fibres begin to form between them.

questions.question: Give an example of a tissue that could be produced by mitosis in a plant.
questions.answer: Xylem tissue (phloem or epidermis are also acceptable).
steps: Mitosis in plant meristems produces new cells that can differentiate.
Those cells can differentiate into xylem vessels or phloem sieve tubes.
Xylem vessels form from specialised cells derived from meristematic divisions.
Epidermis is another tissue formed from mitotic cells.

questions.question: Give one role, other than growth or repair, for new cells produced by mitosis.
questions.answer: Asexual reproduction, producing genetically identical offspring (e.g. budding or vegetative propagation).
steps: Mitosis copies the genome exactly into each daughter cell.
In asexual reproduction, new cells form a genetically identical individual or clone.
Asexual reproduction does not involve meiosis or fertilisation.
Examples include budding in yeast and vegetative propagation in plants.

questions.question: Which statements about sperm cells are correct? 1 sperm cells are diploid; 2 the flagellum rotates using energy; 3 sperm cells have a streamlined shape to increase resistance. Options: A 1, 2 and 3; B 1 and 2 only; C 2 and 3 only; D 2 only.
questions.answer: D (2 only).
steps: Sperm cells are haploid, with one set of chromosomes, so statement 1 is wrong.
The flagellum rotates using ATP from the mitochondria in the midpiece, so statement 2 is correct.
Sperm cells are haploid because they are gametes made by meiosis.
A streamlined shape reduces resistance, not increases it, so statement 3 is wrong.

questions.question: Describe how the nucleus of a sperm cell enters an egg cell.
questions.answer: The sperm binds to the egg, acrosin digests the zona pellucida, and the sperm and egg membranes fuse so the sperm nucleus enters the egg cytoplasm.
steps: The sperm binds to the zona pellucida and egg surface membrane using specific receptor proteins.
The acrosome releases acrosin and other enzymes that digest a path through the zona pellucida.
The sperm cell surface membrane fuses with the egg cell surface membrane.
The sperm nucleus passes into the egg cytoplasm, while the tail stays outside.

questions.topic: RER and Golgi in Enzyme Production
questions.question: Describe the role of the rough endoplasmic reticulum and the Golgi apparatus in the production of the enzymes in cortical granules.
questions.answer: Ribosomes on the rough ER make the enzyme polypeptides, which are carried in vesicles to the Golgi; the Golgi modifies and packages them into cortical granules.
steps: Ribosomes on the rough ER translate mRNA into the enzyme polypeptide, which enters the ER lumen.
Transport vesicles carry the polypeptide from the rough ER to the Golgi apparatus.
The enzymes are then packaged into cortical granules that move to the cell surface.
The Golgi modifies the enzyme and packages it into cortical granules (secretory vesicles).

questions.question: Suggest how the cortical granule enzymes prevent more than one sperm nucleus entering the egg cell.
questions.answer: The enzymes are released by exocytosis and change the zona pellucida, so other sperm cannot bind or fuse with the egg.
steps: When one sperm fuses with the egg, the cortical granules move to and fuse with the egg surface membrane.
They release their enzymes by exocytosis into the space around the egg.
The enzymes modify the zona pellucida, so other sperm can no longer bind to it.
Other sperm are blocked, so only one sperm nucleus enters the egg.

questions.question: From the electron micrograph of an organelle (options A formation of lysosomes, B formation of microtubules, C formation of ribosomal RNA, D formation of vesicles), state the correct function.
questions.answer: B: formation of microtubules
steps: The two views show a short cylinder with parallel ridges, and a ring made of nine triplets of dots (microtubules).
This is a centriole, which has a 9 + 0 triplet arrangement of microtubules.
Centrioles organise the formation of microtubules (spindle fibres), so the answer is B.

questions.question: Suggest why the two views of the organelle in the electron micrographs look different.
questions.answer: The two views are sections cut at different angles: one lengthways (side view) and one across (end view).
steps: A centriole is a three-dimensional cylinder, and the electron microscope shows a thin slice of it.
A section cut along its length shows the cylinder with parallel microtubule lines, while a section cut across it shows a ring of nine triplets.

questions.question: Draw the cell shown in telophase so that it shows metaphase of mitosis.
questions.answer: Draw one large cell with no nuclear envelope, a spindle between two centrioles at the poles, and four X-shaped chromosomes (two long, two short) lined up across the middle (equator).
steps: Draw a single undivided cell (an oval or circle, without the narrow waist), because cytokinesis has not started.
Draw the four chromosomes each as two sister chromatids joined at a centromere (X shape), with two long and two short, and shade them like those in the telophase cell.
Place the centromeres in a line across the middle of the cell, with no nuclear envelope.
Draw spindle fibres from the centrioles at the two poles to the centromeres.

questions.question: Describe what happens in anaphase of mitosis.
questions.answer: Centromeres divide and sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles by shortening spindle fibres.
steps: The centromeres divide, separating each pair of sister chromatids.
Spindle fibres attached to the centromeres shorten and pull the chromatids apart.
Anaphase is the stage where chromatids separate, and telophase follows.
The separated chromatids (now chromosomes) move towards opposite poles of the cell.

questions.question: Using the diagram of relative proportions of the cell cycle, and given that cytokinesis takes 20 minutes, calculate how long interphase takes in hours.
questions.answer: 6 hours
steps: Cytokinesis is 15 degrees of the circle and takes 20 minutes, so 1 degree = 20 / 15 = 1.33 minutes.
Interphase is 270 degrees = 270 x 1.33 = 360 minutes.
360 minutes = 6 hours.

questions.question: State how the mitotic index of a tissue could be calculated.
questions.answer: Mitotic index = number of cells in mitosis / total number of cells x 100.
steps: Count the cells in mitosis under the microscope.
Count the total number of cells in the same field of view.
Counting several fields of view gives a more reliable value.
Divide the number in mitosis by the total and multiply by 100.

questions.question: Complete the labelled sperm cell diagram by drawing and labelling a flagellum and an acrosome.
questions.answer: Draw a long thin tail (flagellum) continuing from the left end of the midpiece, and a cap (acrosome) over the front tip of the head on the right; label both.
steps: The midpiece is on the left and the head is on the right, so draw the flagellum as a long, thin tail extending to the left from the end of the midpiece, and label it flagellum.
Draw the acrosome as a small cap over the front tip of the head (the right end), and label it acrosome.

questions.question: Give the function of the mitochondria in the midpiece of the sperm.
questions.answer: They carry out aerobic respiration to make ATP, which powers movement of the flagellum.
steps: Mitochondria in the midpiece carry out aerobic respiration.
This releases energy to make ATP.
Without this ATP the sperm could not swim effectively.
ATP powers the motor proteins that make the flagellum rotate, so the sperm can swim to the egg.

questions.question: Give two conclusions that can be drawn from the graph of midpiece length against swimming speed of mouse sperm cells.
questions.answer: Males that mate with more than one female have faster sperm than those that mate with one female; there is a weak positive correlation between midpiece length and swimming speed.
steps: Sperm from males that mate with more than one female swim faster on average (about 6.8 um s^-1, crosses) than those from males that mate with only one female (about 5.6 um s^-1, dots).
In both groups there is a weak positive correlation: longer midpiece goes with faster swimming speed, probably because there are more mitochondria making ATP, but the points are widely scattered.
The midpiece lengths of the two groups overlap (about 21.3 to 22.6 um), so midpiece length alone does not explain the difference in speed.

questions.question: Give the name of a statistical test that could assess the strength of the relationship between midpiece length and swimming speed of sperm cells.
questions.answer: Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (or Pearson's correlation coefficient for linear data).
steps: Both variables are continuous measurements, so a correlation test is suitable.
Pearson's correlation coefficient measures the strength of a linear relationship.
Spearman rank correlation gives a value between -1 and +1.
Spearman's rank correlation is used when the data are not normally distributed.
